name: Whirlwind ferrite-core memory
description: Random-access computer memory using magnetized ferrite cores to store individual bits.

date.label: August 1953
date.basis: Date or stated historical interval in cited source; see caveats.

events.statement: MIT’s Whirlwind project demonstrated a 32-by-32 core plane in August 1953.

evidence.supports: Museum dates the 1024-core Whirlwind plane demonstration to August 1953 and identifies MIT, Navy and Forrester.

contributions.resource: Major funder of the wider Whirlwind project by the time of the SAGE programme.

evidence.supports: The National Research Council reports Air Force became major sponsor and 1953 core installation followed.
Museum dates the 1024-core Whirlwind plane demonstration to August 1953 and identifies MIT, Navy and Forrester.

events.caveats: The cited Air Force sponsorship concerns the wider Whirlwind project through SAGE; it does not establish a separately earmarked grant for this core-memory demonstration.

date.basis: Date or stated historical interval in cited source; see caveats.

events.statement: IBM announced the 737 core memory unit for rental at $6,100 a month.

evidence.supports: Museum dates commercial 737 announcement and monthly rental.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest dated witness established by the cited source for this scoped record, not a claim of global first.

measures.money_context: Nominal 1954 monthly rental, not inflation adjusted.
measures.subject: IBM 737 core memory unit
measures.conditions: Museum retrospective; announced unit held 4,096 36-bit words.

caveats: Earlier magnetic-core work by Wang, Rajchman and others is acknowledged by the source; this is a particular operational development path.

research.note: Independent reader checked the museum’s demonstration and 737 rental claims and the National Research Council’s project-wide funding account; no separate memory-specific grant is inferred.
